approvedBy: Comparison draft — not approved for publication

cards.headline: Same violation. Why different outcomes?
body: Both served alcohol to minors. Their suspensions differed.
cards.takeaway: The established facts and prior mitigation made the difference.
cards.design: Premium editorial cover: one restaurant storefront and a suspension notice; two lower labels contrast the historic Busan and Seoul outcomes. Restrained navy, ivory and subtle gold; both outcomes clearly marked as historic.

cards.headline: Same violation. Different appeal decisions.

body.text: The panel weighed no similar prior breach, a prosecutorial non-indictment decision and the small business size, cutting 2 months to 15 days.
The agency had already cut 2 months to 1 month after the prosecutor declined to indict. The appeal panel upheld that reduced sanction.

cards.takeaway: Check which mitigating circumstances the agency already considered.
cards.design: Two equal columns with restrained old-versus-revised sanction markers. Use Busan and Seoul location labels, but no invented ratings, faces, quotes or restaurant identity; footer identifies these as historic administrative appeals.

cards.headline: Current rule: 7 days for a first violation

body.text: First violation: the current standard for serving alcohol to minors at a restaurant.
Second violation of the same conduct: the current standard suspension.
Third violation of the same conduct: a two-month suspension.

cards.takeaway: The pre-2024 first-offense standard of 2 months is no longer the current rule.
cards.design: Three bold number rows read top-down, with 7 days given the strongest typographic weight. A small 2024 amendment marker differentiates current law from the historic case outcomes.

cards.headline: A misused ID may trigger exemption, not a cut

body.text: Video, testimony or other proof must show a forged, altered or misused ID hid the patron’s age, or violence or threats blocked an age check.
Looking older or non-indictment alone is insufficient. A final guilty verdict bars the evidence-based routes, except where sentencing was deferred.

cards.takeaway: When the legal conditions are met, the sanction must be waived.
cards.design: Evidence-versus-assertion composition: ID card and CCTV still on the left, two legal-condition panels on the right. A clear exception footer; do not render exemption as automatic solely from an ID check.

cards.headline: Non-indictment does not guarantee a reduction

body.text: A minor breach or slight oversight without intent may qualify for mitigation.
For deferred prosecution or sentencing, the violation must lack intent or pose no public-health risk.
If eligible, the agency may cut the period by up to one-half; it is not automatic.

cards.takeaway: Criminal and administrative decisions are separate.
cards.design: Three vertically stepped panels: nature of breach, prosecutor/court outcome plus conditions, and agency discretion. Use a modest gavel icon; emphasize MAY reduce rather than a guaranteed halving.

cards.headline: Three expired noodle packs: 15 days to 7

body.text: Three packs kept to cook or sell, one day expired
Breach upheld; severity weighed for mitigation

cards.takeaway: One day past expiry does not entitle every restaurant to the same seven-day result.
cards.design: Two proportional horizontal bars beginning at zero with exactly 15 and 7 days. Small unobtrusive noodle-pack illustration, not a fabricated case photo; keep original violation and mitigation distinct.

cards.headline: A second inspection is not automatically a second offense
body: Compare the conduct and the dates of the earlier sanction and later violation.
cards.design: High-contrast editorial breathing card. One large centered sentence with a three-point timeline at the bottom. Allow generous margins; it must read as a single insight, not a checklist.

cards.headline: Could a monetary penalty replace closure?

body.text: First and second alcohol-to-minors violations may qualify, subject to legal conditions.
Third violations and unpaid surcharges are generally excluded; limited exceptions may apply.
The daily amount reflects prior-year gross sales and the suspension period.

cards.takeaway: The operator cannot choose a fine unilaterally; the agency decides.
cards.design: Contrasting calendar and monetary assessment document. Reading order: eligibility, exclusion, revenue-based amount. Avoid presenting the substitution as a personal right or as a criminal fine.

cards.headline: Pre-notice received? Four records to check

body.text: Check the breach, offense count, planned suspension and deadline.
Match any ID check on CCTV to the order and payment times.
Was the earlier sanction for the same act, and on what date?
Why was indictment suspended, and did the agency note it?

cards.takeaway: Preserve relevant CCTV footage before deletion, where possible.
cards.design: Save-worthy evidence cross-check sheet: four document tiles with unmistakable icons and hierarchy. Micro-labels show what each record can establish; avoid treating payment records as proof of age.

cards.headline: What can you prepare or have drafted?

body.text: Have the notice or final order, any CCTV or payment records, earlier orders and the prosecutor’s decision, if available.
If retained, Ethos Administrative Attorney Office may compare records and draft agency submissions. Filing is limited by law; scope and fees are separately agreed.

cards.takeaway: A free initial review covers the stage and first records.
cards.design: Two document panels with different purposes: items the operator can supply versus paid agency-document preparation within legal scope. A single plain-text line for free initial screening; no button, URL, direct contact or guaranteed relief.
